name: Mount Sharp boxwork terrain, Gale Crater (2 km x 2 km)

risk_model.description: Estimated risk = slope / 20 deg x 100. Cells at or above 20 deg are impassable: NASA's xEVA suit capability is walking on slopes of up to 20 deg (EVA-EXP-0075, written for lunar missions). Slope is taken from the 1 m elevation model after 1.5 m Gaussian smoothing; each 2 m cell keeps its steepest value. Rocks and loose sand are not in the model yet. Data layers: Ground the Curiosity rover drove on (-20 risk points); No radio line of sight to the habitat (+20 risk points); Boxwork ridges (+15 risk points); Radiation shelter (terrain blocks the sky) (+0 risk points). Combined risk = slope risk + sum of weight x layer score / 100, kept within 0-100; layer weights are our assumptions. Layers never make an impassable cell passable.
risk_model.layers_formula: risk = clamp(slope / limit x 100 + sum(weight x layer / 100), 0, 100)

sources.mission: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (stereo), tied to MGS MOLA
sources.instrument: HiRISE, with CTX and HRSC where HiRISE stereo is missing
sources.cannot_see: Features smaller than a few metres. Individual rocks and the crests of narrow ridges are smoothed out.
Rocks smaller than about 1 m. Loose sand cannot be told apart from firm ground. Shown here at 0.5 m per pixel.
Only where the rover stopped; the ground between waypoints is not recorded.

layers.label: Ground the Curiosity rover drove on
layers.description: Cells within 3 m of Curiosity's driven track. A 900 kg rover crossed this ground, so it is firm and passable at rover scale.
layers.cannot_see: Only one track across the area; ground off the track is not proven either way.

layers.label: No radio line of sight to the habitat
layers.description: Cells where terrain blocks the straight line between a suit radio (2 m above ground) and the habitat antenna (3 m mast, assumed). Out of sight, the astronaut cannot call the habitat directly.
layers.source: Line of sight computed from the MSL Gale merged DEM (USGS Astrogeology), https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/mars_msl_gale_merged_dem_1m
layers.cannot_see: No relay orbiters, rovers or radio bending around ridges; the 2 m elevation grid smooths narrow crests, so a few shadows may be missed.

layers.label: Boxwork ridges
layers.description: Ridge lines found in the orbital image where they cross in many directions, the pattern of boxwork. Each crossing means stepping over a ridge 1-2 m high. Ridges are also the science target of this area.
layers.source: Rule-based ridge detection on the HiRISE colour mosaic (USGS / JPL), https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/mars_msl_gale_merged_orthophoto_mosaic_25cm
layers.cannot_see: Ridge height is not measured, only the line; some layer edges may still be counted and faint ridges under dust are missed. Not checked against rover images ridge by ridge.

layers.label: Radiation shelter (terrain blocks the sky)
layers.effect: map only, not in the route cost
layers.description: Share of the sky hidden by the terrain, shown where it is 15 % or more. Curiosity's RAD measured 4 % less radiation dose next to a butte that blocked 19 % of the sky; scaled the same way, the last measured 0.16 mGy/day falls to about 0.143 mGy/day in the most sheltered spot here. Where to wait out a solar storm.
layers.source: Sky view computed from the MSL Gale merged DEM (USGS Astrogeology); dose scaling from MSL RAD measurements at Murray Buttes, Ehresmann et al. 2021, JGR Planets, https://doi.org/10.1029/2021JE006851
layers.cannot_see: Terrain more than 800 m away or outside the area (such as upper Mount Sharp) is counted as open sky, so shelter is underestimated. The dose scaling comes from a single measured site; solar storm particles are shielded differently from cosmic rays.
